vignette:
Marisol Ortega is a 44-year-old American diplomat who had spent much of the last three years rotating through a U.S. mission in a conflict zone, where military convoys, checkpoints, and negotiations with armed actors were part of ordinary working life. The event she returns to most often took place during what was supposed to be a civilian protection visit. Her vehicle was stopped by armed men at an improvised roadblock, and she was pulled from the car, forced to the ground, and held down while people shouted over her in a language she partly understood. What has stayed with her is not only the fear that she might be killed, but the way she was handled: gripped by the arms, pinned at the shoulders, spoken about rather than spoken to. She remembers thinking, with a kind of stunned clarity, that she had ceased to be a person in that moment and had become something to be moved, inspected, and used.

In the months after she returned to the United States, Marisol found that seemingly unrelated moments could throw her back into that sense of degradation. In her work, military topics are unavoidable; briefings about troop movements, policy discussions about security assistance, even hearing colleagues talk casually about "stabilization" can make her feel abruptly small and hollow. Encounters that involve moral misconduct are also potent. A colleague cutting ethical corners, a senior official dismissing local suffering, or even watching someone behave callously in public can leave her shaken in a way she struggles to explain. What catches her most viscerally, though, is any sensation of being physically constrained: a crowded elevator, a hand on her forearm to guide her through a doorway, a seatbelt locking suddenly when she brakes. In those moments she has come to believe again that she is not fully a person with agency, just an object in other people's hands. The same episodes often bring a more diffuse collapse in meaning; she can leave a meeting on arms policy thinking that none of what she does matters and doubting her own judgment, uncertain that she could trust herself to do the right thing under pressure.

Those conclusions have not remained fleeting. Marisol has spent long evenings in her apartment replaying the roadside detention and turning over the same question-why this happened to her, why she was there, what it says about her. She tells herself she is trying to understand it, but the thinking rarely arrives anywhere new. Instead, the more she circles around its meaning, the more fixed she becomes on the idea that something essential in her has been altered: that life no longer carries the sense of purpose it once did, and that she cannot rely on herself in morally difficult situations. At other times she pushes in the opposite direction and tries hard not to think about the incident at all, cutting off images midstream and forcing herself back into work. That effort comes from the same place: she is frightened by how quickly the memory strips away her sense of dignity, and she is desperate not to feel like that objectified version of herself again.

Over time, these habits have made her world narrower and more reactive. Because she spends so much energy suppressing trauma-related thoughts, ordinary reminders seem to break through with more force. A routine policy memo about military aid can suddenly feel invasive, as if it has bypassed all her defenses. After hours of ruminating about the meaning of what happened, she becomes more sensitive to signs of wrongdoing in others, reading them through the lens of what she endured and feeling freshly contaminated by human cruelty. At work she has started avoiding some security meetings when she can delegate them, and when she cannot, she sits near exits and stiffens if anyone reaches toward her chair. Her role as a diplomat requires composure and nuanced judgment, yet she now leaves certain meetings flooded with self-doubt, reviewing whether she said the right thing, whether she missed some ethical failure, whether she can trust herself at all.

Marisol is single and lives alone, and the isolation has given these patterns room to harden. She still functions at a high level by external measures, but her life feels increasingly organized around bracing for reminders and managing the aftermath of them. She sought help only after a recent incident in the embassy annex, when a crowded security screening line stalled and the agent behind her placed a hand at her elbow to move her forward. She froze, felt instantly reduced and unreal, and later spent the night going over why such a small contact could undo her. What frightened her most was not just the intensity of the reaction but the conviction that the work that once defined her no longer means anything, and that she may no longer be someone she can trust. What she hopes, cautiously, is to find a way to be in her body and in her work again without feeling at the mercy of every reminder.
